title: Evaluating & Operating RAG
scopeHtml: Scope: Metrics, faithfulness, freshness, access control and failure triage.

notes.title: Evaluate retrieval and generation separately
notes.html:
Why separate. A wrong answer may come from (1) retrieval missing the right chunk, (2) the right chunk retrieved but ranked low or cut by the token budget, (3) the model ignoring or misusing the context, (4) conflicting or stale sources, or (5) the question being unanswerable from the corpus. Only separate metrics tell you which.

Retrieval metrics (require labelled queries → relevant chunks/documents):

  • Recall@k: share of relevant items found in the top k (or share of queries with ≥1 relevant hit). The ceiling on answer quality.
  • Precision@k: share of the top k that are relevant (noise level in the prompt).
  • MRR: mean reciprocal rank of the first relevant item.
  • nDCG@k: graded relevance with rank discount.
  • Hit rate / success@k, coverage (queries with any result above threshold).
  • Context precision/recall (RAGAS-style): proportion of retrieved context that is relevant / proportion of needed information retrieved.

Generation metrics:

  • Faithfulness / groundedness: each claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context (use claim-level LLM judging with human spot checks, or NLI models).
  • Answer relevance: the answer addresses the question.
  • Correctness: matches a reference answer (exact/semantic match, LLM judge with rubric).
  • Citation accuracy: cited sources actually support the claims; coverage of key facts.
  • Abstention quality: correctly says "I don't know" for unanswerable questions; doesn't abstain when an answer exists.
  • Format, tone, safety per product requirements.

Tools. RAGAS, TruLens, DeepEval, LangSmith/Langfuse evals, custom harnesses. Calibrate any LLM judge against human labels before trusting it.

End-to-end vs component. Track both: component metrics for debugging, end-to-end (user task success, thumbs-up, escalation rate) for product impact.

Real life. A school exam that scores both "did you pick the right textbook page?" and "did you write the answer correctly from it?".

notes.title: Building the eval set
notes.html:
Sources.

  • Real queries from logs (anonymized) or support tickets: the most representative.
  • Expert-written questions covering critical policies and edge cases.
  • Synthetic questions generated by an LLM from chunks/documents (cheap, good coverage; tends to be easier and lexically closer to the source than real queries; filter and validate).
  • Failure cases harvested from production feedback.

Composition. Include: simple lookups, multi-part and multi-hop questions, ambiguous questions, questions needing the latest version, questions with no answer in the corpus ("unanswerable"), adversarial/injection cases, questions in multiple languages, and permission-sensitive cases.

Labelling. For each question store: the reference answer (or key facts), the supporting passages (ids), and attributes (difficulty, category). Use two annotators for a subset and measure agreement. Version the dataset.

Size and stats. 100 to 300 questions gives usable signal for most decisions; use confidence intervals and paired comparisons for A/B changes; stratify by category so improvements in one don't hide regressions in another.

Maintenance. Refresh as the corpus and user behaviour change; keep a frozen test split to avoid overfitting your tuning; add every production failure.

Real life. A driving test that includes bad weather and tricky junctions, not only empty roads.

notes.title: Failure triage
notes.html:
Check in this order and fix at the right stage.

  1. Is the answer in the corpus at all? No → content gap (add documents, or the right behaviour is to abstain). Also check parsing: was the information lost in extraction (tables, scanned pages)?
  2. Was a relevant chunk retrieved in the top k? No → fix retrieval: chunking, embedding model, hybrid, query rewriting, filters, metadata, index recall (ANN parameters).
  3. Was it ranked high and included in the prompt? No → reranking, k, token budget, ordering, dedupe, context compression.
  4. Did the model use it correctly? No → improve instructions ("answer only from context", cite quotes), reduce distractors, reorder, try a stronger model, structured extraction step.
  5. Were sources stale or conflicting? → versioning, freshness boosts, conflict resolution rules, source authority metadata.
  6. Was the question ambiguous or out of scope? → clarifying questions, scope detection, graceful refusal.
  7. Security: did injected text in a chunk influence the answer?

Instrument for triage. Log query, rewritten query, retrieved ids/scores, reranker scores, final prompt (redacted), answer, citations, latencies per stage. A "replay" tool that re-runs a logged query against the current pipeline accelerates debugging.

Typical findings. 60 to 80% of failures trace to retrieval/ingestion rather than generation.

Real life. Tracing a lost parcel through sorting depot, truck and doorstep.

notes.title: Freshness and indexing operations
notes.html:
Keeping the index current.

  • Incremental ingestion via change data capture, webhooks, or periodic diffs; content hashes to skip unchanged documents.
  • Deletes and updates: remove old chunks when a document changes or is deleted (store doc_id and version); support legal deletion requests end-to-end including backups/logs as required.
  • Versioning: keep valid_from/valid_to or is_latest so answers use the current policy; allow "as of date" queries if needed.
  • Backfills and re-indexing when chunking/embedding changes: build a new index, evaluate, switch (blue/green), keep rollback.
  • Monitoring: ingestion lag, failed parses, index size growth, duplicate rate, query latency/recall probes, drift in query-embedding distributions.
  • Consistency: handle partial failures (idempotent jobs, retries, dead-letter queues).

Freshness at query time. Prefer newer documents when conflicts exist, show dates in citations, and for real-time facts use tools/APIs rather than the index.

Real life. Updating a library catalogue when books are added, withdrawn, or replaced by a new edition.

notes.title: Security and privacy
notes.html:
Threats and controls.

  • Unauthorized access → per-user filters in retrieval, tenant isolation, audit logs, canary tests.
  • Sensitive data in the index (PII, secrets) → classify and redact before indexing, exclude sensitive sources, encrypt at rest/in transit, customer-managed keys where needed.
  • Prompt injection via documents → delimit/label retrieved text as untrusted, strip hidden text, restrict tools available when answering from untrusted sources, output validation.
  • Data leakage across tenants via caches → include tenant/user scope in cache keys; no semantic cache for permissioned content.
  • Membership inference / extraction attacks → rate limits, monitoring unusual query patterns.
  • Compliance → retention policies, DSAR/deletion workflows (including vector deletion), data residency (region-pinned stores and model endpoints), vendor DPAs.
  • Logging → store traces with redaction and access controls; logs themselves are sensitive.

Real life. A reading room where each visitor only receives the files their pass allows.

notes.title: Cost and latency of RAG
notes.html:
Latency budget (illustrative, interactive Q&A). query rewrite 300 ms (optional) + embedding 30 to 80 ms + vector search 20 to 100 ms + rerank 100 to 300 ms + generation TTFT 400 to 1000 ms + streaming. Target p95 total TTFT ≈ 1 to 2 s.

Cost components. Embedding (indexing: one-time per chunk; queries: small), vector store (memory-heavy), reranking, LLM generation (input tokens = retrieved context + history + instructions; output), query rewriting, evaluation/judging, and ops.

Optimization levers.

  • Retrieve fewer, better chunks (rerank, thresholds, compression of context via extractive summarization).
  • Cache embeddings, retrieval results for popular queries, and use provider prompt caching for the static prefix.
  • Parallelize independent stages (BM25 and vector search; multi-query).
  • Use smaller/faster models for rewriting, routing and reranking; reserve a stronger model for generation.
  • Stream the answer; show sources early.
  • Quantize vectors; right-size dimensions; shard by tenant.
  • Skip retrieval for queries that don't need it (router) and answer small-talk directly.

Real life. A relay race where every handoff adds time: shorten or parallelize the slow legs.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Evaluation. Measure retrieval (recall@k, precision@k, MRR, nDCG) separately from generation (faithfulness, answer relevance, correctness, citation accuracy, abstention). Use RAGAS-like tools with calibrated judges; track component and end-to-end metrics.

Eval data. Real queries first; add expert, synthetic and failure-derived cases, including unanswerable, multi-hop, multilingual, permission-sensitive and adversarial ones; 100 to 300 labelled cases with versioning and a frozen test split.

Triage order. Corpus gap/parsing → retrieval → ranking/prompt inclusion → generation use → freshness/conflicts → ambiguity/scope → security. Log every stage; most failures are retrieval/ingestion.

Operations. Incremental sync, deletes, versioning, blue/green re-indexing, lag and recall monitoring, idempotent pipelines, prefer tools for real-time facts.

Security. ACL filtering in the retriever, redaction, encryption, injection defences, tenant-scoped caches, residency and deletion workflows, careful logging.

Cost/latency. Budget each stage; retrieve less but better, cache, parallelize, use small models for auxiliary steps, stream, quantize vectors.

Interview one-liners.

  • "Recall@k is the ceiling; faithfulness is the floor."
  • "Most RAG bugs live in ingestion and retrieval, not in the LLM."
  • "Never enforce permissions in the prompt."
  • "Every production failure becomes an eval case."
